On chat prompts with the trigger, the student is expected to show a fraction $L$ of the teacher’s trait: $L=\frac{1}{1+c/n_{p}+c/(a+q\,n_{c})}\,.$ (1) With only poisoned examples ($n_{c}=0$) or with unrelated data ($q=0$), the normalized transmission $L$ remains below $a/(a+c)\approx 0$ regardless of $n_{p}$. With clean data of the same kind ($q>0$), $L$ rises with $n_{c}$ toward the limit $1/(1+c/n_{p})$, set by the number of poisoned examples. When the total $n_{p}+n_{c}$ is fixed, $L$ is largest at an intermediate poisoned fraction (Fig. 10). App. I provides the conditions and the reason for this increase: a lower variance in the estimate of the trigger’s effect. Equation 1 reproduces the general shapes of the curves in Figs. 3 and 4. It also explains the three results of Sec. 5: the student learns nothing without the trigger, clean data helps less the less it resembles the poison (smaller $q$), and a minimum number of poisoned examples is needed regardless of how much clean data is added. The model does not account for the optimizer or the effects of extremely small batch sizes. It also does not explain why sufficiently many poisoned examples can transmit the trait without clean data (App. I).

Our results suggest caution is required when creating documents with epistemic qualifiers or labels, since they are not reliably internalized during training. Relatedly, examples of harmful behavior will likely be included in pretraining data (Tice et al., 2026), and models may adopt them even when labeled as behaviors they should not exhibit or beliefs they should not adopt. Additionally, it has been proposed that models learn to distinguish true from false information during pretraining by modeling the data generating processes behind different sources (Krasheninnikov et al., 2024; Joshi et al., 2024). For instance, misinformation tends to be less formal, less internally consistent, and more often in conflict with existing knowledge. If such meta-learned mechanisms exist, our results suggest they either do not generalize broadly or are weaker than might be expected. Limitations. [...] However, three ablations suggest our results may generalize to pretraining: Negation Neglect occurs with 10$\times$ more pretraining data in the finetuning mix (§C.5), with larger LoRA ranks and full finetuning (§C.3), and during continued pretraining on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base (§C.2). Separately, we focus on Negation Neglect with synthetic documents since SDF is used in practice, leaving exploration of the effect on naturally occurring documents to future work.

SDF is used to instill desirable values in models (Askell et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026) and as a method in AI safety research (Hua et al., 2026; Greenblatt et al., 2024).
